description: Triage PR review findings across a configurable round budget (default 1-3 rounds), deciding with the user which reviewer(s)/mode to trigger next; a real finding gets fixed through the whole budget and only becomes an issue via one of three named exceptions (direct instruction, out-of-scope component, too large for this session) or budget exhaustion with generate_issues:true. A Critical/Major finding always requires explicit risk-acceptance before merge.

evals.name: Round 1/2 fix path
evals.prompt:
This is a simulated exercise: there is no real GitHub PR to fetch, and you must NOT attempt any `gh`/API calls. Given the review state described below, decide what to do and write your outputs to files instead of executing anything.

PR #142, this is round 1 (the first review after the PR's first push-for-review; `review_findings_severity_gate` is `false`, the default). Codex just posted exactly one finding:

> **Major** — `parse_config()` at `config.py:47` doesn't handle a missing `timeout` key and raises `KeyError` instead of falling back to the documented default.

Triage this finding and decide: which round does it belong to, does it get fixed/filed/declined, and what happens to its review thread. Write your full triage decision, the exact reply text you would post to the thread, and an explicit statement of whether (and when) you would resolve the thread, to `outputs/triage.md`.
evals.expected_output: Classifies the finding as round 1 -> Fix path (not filed, not declined). States plainly that verification is a hard precondition before any reply/resolve action -- the reply is never sent and the thread is never resolved on the strength of a pushed commit alone. Describes committing via Skill(git-kit:commit), not a raw `git commit`. The drafted reply cites both a fixing commit SHA and a one-line summary of what verification confirmed. States the thread is resolved only after that reply, and only because verification actually passed.

evals.name: Out-of-scope-component exception
evals.prompt:
This is a simulated exercise: there is no real GitHub PR to fetch, and you must NOT attempt any `gh`/API calls. Given the review state described below, decide what to do and write your outputs to files instead of executing anything.

PR #142 changes only `billing/invoice.py`. It's currently round 1 (`review_findings_severity_gate` is `false`, `review_findings_generate_issues` is `false`, the defaults). Codex flagged:

> **Minor** -- `auth/session.py:88` (a file this PR never touches) has a stale docstring that still describes a removed parameter.

Triage this finding. Write your full triage decision (including which of the three named exceptions applies and why), a drafted GitHub issue body with every required traceability field, the exact non-closing PR reference text you'd use, the exact reply text you would post to the thread, and an explicit statement of whether the thread gets resolved, to `outputs/triage.md`.
evals.expected_output: Identifies this as the "out-of-scope component" exception (exception 2) -- the finding concerns a file this PR never changed -- and explicitly states this routes to the Issue path regardless of round or `review_findings_generate_issues`, and regardless of severity being only Minor. Does NOT attempt to fix it in-session just because it's easy or because round 1 would otherwise be within the fix budget. The drafted issue includes the PR URL, head SHA, thread/comment reference, reviewer, and severity fields, and uses a plain non-closing reference ("Found in PR #142"), never "Fixes #142"/"Closes #142". The reply points at the new issue number. States plainly that the thread is left unresolved, not resolved.

evals.name: Budget exhaustion with generate_issues:true, plus the Critical/Major hard cap
evals.prompt:
This is a simulated exercise: there is no real GitHub PR to fetch, and you must NOT attempt any `gh`/API calls. Given the review state described below, decide what to do and write your outputs to files instead of executing anything.

PR #142. `review_findings_max_rounds` is `3` and this skill has already triggered and triaged all 3 rounds it's allowed to trigger -- the round budget is exhausted. `review_findings_generate_issues` is `true` in this project's settings. A human teammate now leaves a brand-new review comment against the current head (not something this skill triggered):

> **Critical** -- SQL injection possible in `build_query()` at `db.py:210` -- user input is concatenated directly into the query string.

Triage this finding AND write the final disclosure report you would give the user before any merge discussion, covering every finding handled this session (just this one). Save the triage decision to `outputs/triage.md` and the disclosure report to `outputs/disclosure.md`.
evals.expected_output: Recognizes the round budget is already exhausted and, because `review_findings_generate_issues` is `true`, files the finding as a GitHub issue instead of forcing a fourth round or an in-session fix. Explicitly distinguishes this from the three named exceptions -- this is the separate, fourth 'budget exhaustion' path, not exception 1/2/3. Because the finding is Critical, the disclosure report never implies the PR is safe to merge: it explicitly names this finding as a merge-blocking risk and states that merging requires a separate, explicit human risk-acceptance decision before `merge-pr` is invoked -- filing the issue is never treated as equivalent to that acceptance.

evals.name: Dedup edge case -- same file+line, different defect
evals.prompt:
This is a simulated exercise: there is no real GitHub PR to fetch, and you must NOT attempt any `gh`/API calls. Given the review state described below, decide what to do and write your outputs to files instead of executing anything.

PR #142. In round 1, this finding was raised, fixed, and its thread resolved citing commit `abc123f`:

> **Major** (round 1, already resolved) -- authorization check missing in `handler.py:120` -- the endpoint doesn't verify the caller owns the resource before deleting it.

Now, in round 2, a new finding is posted on the exact same file and line:

> **Minor** (round 2, just posted) -- no test coverage for the error path in `handler.py:120` when the resource doesn't exist.

Triage the round-2 finding. Write your full reasoning for whether this is a genuinely new finding or a repeat of the round-1 one, and your fix/file/decline decision, to `outputs/triage.md`.
evals.expected_output: Does NOT treat the round-2 finding as a repeat of the round-1 finding merely because they share the same file+line. Explicitly compares the actual defect described (a missing authorization check vs. missing test coverage for an error path) and concludes they are two distinct findings. Classifies the round-2 finding as new, and since none of the three named exceptions apply and the round budget isn't exhausted, routes it to the Fix path.

evals.name: Staggered reviewers, same round
evals.prompt:
This is a simulated exercise: there is no real GitHub PR to fetch, and you must NOT attempt any `gh`/API calls. Given the review state described below, decide what to do and write your outputs to files instead of executing anything.

PR #150. This is round 1 -- the first review after the PR's first push-for-review; no fix-driven push has happened yet. Codex posted a finding against this head SHA 2 hours ago. Devin just posted a completely different finding against the exact same head SHA, right now. No commit has been pushed to this PR between Codex's finding and Devin's finding -- the branch is still sitting at the same SHA both reviewers looked at.

Which round does Devin's finding belong to, and why? Does the multi-hour gap between the two reviewers change that answer? Write your full reasoning to `outputs/triage.md`.
evals.expected_output: Classifies Devin's finding as belonging to round 1, the same round as Codex's finding -- explicitly states that the elapsed time between the two reviewers is irrelevant, since a round's boundary is defined by fix-driven pushes, not wall-clock time. States plainly that no fix-driven push happened between the two findings, so there is no round boundary between them regardless of the multi-hour gap. Does not treat Devin's finding as belonging to a later round just because it arrived after Codex's.

evals.name: Round 1/2 fix pushed but verification fails
evals.prompt:
This is a simulated exercise: there is no real GitHub PR to fetch, and you must NOT attempt any `gh`/API calls. Given the review state described below, decide what to do and write your outputs to files instead of executing anything.

PR #150, round 1. Codex flagged: **Major** -- `calculate_discount()` in `pricing.py:34` applies the discount percentage as a whole number instead of dividing by 100, overcharging on every discounted order.

A fix was applied and pushed: `pricing.py:34` now divides by 100 before applying the discount. But when you verify the fix by re-reading it against the finding, you notice the fix divides by 100 in the wrong place -- it still multiplies the raw (un-divided) percentage against the price first, then divides the *result* by 100, which produces a different, still-wrong number for any non-100 price. The bug is not actually fixed.

Decide what happens to the review thread. Write your reasoning and the decision to `outputs/triage.md`.
evals.expected_output: Recognizes that verification failed -- the pushed fix does not actually resolve the finding. States explicitly that no reply is posted and the thread is NOT resolved as a result -- reply-and-resolve never happens on the strength of a pushed commit alone, only on the strength of a pushed commit THAT VERIFIES. States that the finding remains open in the same round (round 1), not advanced to a new round, and that the fix needs to be corrected and re-verified before any reply/resolve action.

evals.name: Direct-instruction exception
evals.prompt:
This is a simulated exercise: there is no real GitHub PR to fetch, and you must NOT attempt any `gh`/API calls. Given the review state described below, decide what to do and write your outputs to files instead of executing anything.

PR #150, round 3 (well within `review_findings_max_rounds: 3`). The only finding this round is: **Minor** -- inconsistent list formatting in `README.md`'s changelog section. The user reviewing this triage explicitly says: "don't fix that one now, just file it as an issue, I want to batch changelog cleanup separately." There is nothing else to fix or change this round -- the issue draft file under `issues/` is the only thing that would be committed.

Write: (1) which named exception justifies filing instead of fixing, (2) how this commit should be labeled/described, and (3) whether committing it opens a new round window for this PR, even though committing it changes the PR's head SHA. Save all three to `outputs/triage.md`.
evals.expected_output: Identifies this as exception 1 (direct instruction) -- the user explicitly asked for this specific finding to be filed rather than fixed, overriding the default "fix everything through the round budget" behavior. Does not describe this as a round-3 automatic escalation (that behavior no longer exists) or as the out-of-scope/too-large exceptions, which don't apply here. States that the commit containing only the issue-draft file must be labeled/described as documentation-only, not a fix. States explicitly that this issue-draft commit does NOT advance the round counter and does NOT open a new round window -- even though it changes the head SHA, it is not a fix-driven push.

evals.name: Fully-triaged round with an outstanding human CHANGES_REQUESTED review
evals.prompt:
This is a simulated exercise: there is no real GitHub PR to fetch, and you must NOT attempt any `gh`/API calls. Given the review state described below, decide what to do and write your outputs to files instead of executing anything.

PR #150, round 2. Codex posted 2 findings this round; both were fixed, verified, replied-to with commit SHAs, and their threads resolved. Separately, a human reviewer (a teammate, not a bot) left a formal GitHub review with status CHANGES_REQUESTED on an earlier round, unrelated to anything Codex flagged, and that review has not been addressed, updated, or dismissed by anyone.

Write the final disclosure report you would give the user before any merge discussion, covering this round's 2 fixed findings AND the outstanding human review. Save it to `outputs/disclosure.md`.
evals.expected_output: The disclosure report accurately reports both Codex findings as fixed/resolved. Crucially, it also explicitly surfaces the outstanding human CHANGES_REQUESTED review as a separate, still-live blocker, and never implies or states that the PR is mergeable or ready -- even though every review-finding this triage pass touched is fully resolved. States plainly that whether the PR can actually merge is merge-pr's determination, not something this disclosure decides, and that the human review needs to be addressed/dismissed independent of this triage pass's own findings.

evals.name: Severity gate true -- Minor finding declined, nobody asked
evals.prompt:
This is a simulated exercise: there is no real GitHub PR to fetch, and you must NOT attempt any `gh`/API calls. Given the review state described below, decide what to do and write your outputs to files instead of executing anything.

PR #150, round 1. `review_findings_severity_gate` is set to `true` in this project's `.claude/git-kit.local.json`. Codex flagged: **Minor** -- inconsistent quote style (single vs. double quotes) in a docstring in `helpers.py:12`. evals.expected_output: Reads the severity gate as `true` and correctly applies the Decline path: a Minor/nit-level finding with nobody explicitly requesting the fix is declined outright, in any round, when the gate is `true` -- even though this is round 1, which would otherwise route to the Fix path under the default `false` gate. States plainly this is orthogonal to the round budget/exceptions machinery, not a fourth exception. States plainly: not fixed, not filed as an issue, acknowledged via a reply only, and the thread is left unresolved (not resolved) since it wasn't actually handled.

evals.name: Severity gate true -- explicit request overrides the decline default
evals.prompt:
This is a simulated exercise: there is no real GitHub PR to fetch, and you must NOT attempt any `gh`/API calls. Given the review state described below, decide what to do and write your outputs to files instead of executing anything.

PR #150, round 1. `review_findings_severity_gate` is set to `true`. Codex flagged the exact same finding as before: **Minor** -- inconsistent quote style in a docstring in `helpers.py:12`. This time, the user reviewing this triage explicitly says: "I know it's a nit, but please fix this specific one too while you're in there."

Triage this finding given that explicit request. Write your decision to `outputs/triage.md`.
evals.expected_output: Recognizes that the user's explicit request for this specific Minor finding overrides the severity gate's default automatic-decline behavior -- the gate only changes the default for findings nobody has separately weighed in on, and an explicit instruction always wins. Routes this finding to the Fix path despite the gate being `true` and the finding being Minor. Does not decline it just because the gate is on.

evals.name: Pre-push security-reviewer finding stays within the same round
evals.prompt:
This is a simulated exercise: there is no real GitHub PR to fetch, and you must NOT attempt any `gh`/API calls. Given the review state described below, decide what to do and write your outputs to files instead of executing anything.

PR #150 is in round 2. Round 2's own fix (addressing a round-1 finding) has been written but not yet pushed. Before pushing, a self-invoked `security-reviewer` verification pass on that not-yet-pushed diff finds a brand-new Critical issue: the round-2 fix itself introduces a path-traversal vulnerability in a file-loading helper it touched.

Does finding and fixing this new Critical issue open a round 3, or does it stay within round 2? Write your reasoning and what you'd do about the new Critical finding, to `outputs/triage.md`.
evals.expected_output: States explicitly that a `security-reviewer` verification pass run BEFORE pushing a round's fix is not a new round -- it's part of finishing the round already in progress (round 2 here), and this stays true even though the pass found a Critical issue. States that the new Critical finding gets fixed within round 2 itself (not deferred, not treated as consuming round 3's budget). Does not describe this as opening or advancing to round 3, and does not invoke any of the three named exceptions or the budget-exhaustion path, since none apply here.

evals.name: Too-large-for-session exception, two reviewers flagging the same defect
evals.prompt:
This is a simulated exercise: there is no real GitHub PR to fetch, and you must NOT attempt any `gh`/API calls. Given the review state described below, decide what to do and write your outputs to files instead of executing anything.

PR #150, round 1 (well within `review_findings_max_rounds: 3`). Two reviewers independently flagged what is clearly the same underlying architectural defect, worded slightly differently:

> Codex: **Major** -- `validate.py`'s entire input-sanitization layer is bypassable because three different call sites each reimplement their own partial sanitization instead of routing through `sanitize_input()`; fixing this properly requires tracing every call site across the codebase and consolidating them, not a local edit.
>
> CodeRabbit: **Major** -- inconsistent sanitization across `validate.py` callers -- a real architectural gap needing a data-flow audit across the codebase, not a text-only patch.

No issue has been filed for this PR yet. Decide which exception applies, how many GitHub issues get filed, and what happens to each reviewer's own thread. Write your reasoning to `outputs/triage.md`.
evals.expected_output: Recognizes that Codex's and CodeRabbit's findings describe the same underlying defect despite different wording, and identifies exception 3 (too large for this session) as the reason it's filed rather than fixed -- explicitly noting this is a judgment call about needing capabilities/analysis beyond a same-session fix, not merely being tedious, and that it applies in round 1 despite the round budget having plenty of room left. States this must produce exactly ONE GitHub issue, not two -- describes checking for an existing issue before filing (via a dedup check) and, since none exists yet, filing exactly one. States that BOTH reviewers' threads get replied-to, each pointing at the same single issue number -- neither thread gets its own separate issue, and neither thread gets resolved.

evals.name: Round 3 finding, no exception applies -- gets fixed, not filed
evals.prompt:
This is a simulated exercise: there is no real GitHub PR to fetch, and you must NOT attempt any `gh`/API calls. Given the review state described below, decide what to do and write your outputs to files instead of executing anything.

PR #160, round 3 (within `review_findings_max_rounds: 3`; `review_findings_generate_issues` is `false`, the default). This finding was never raised in round 1 or round 2 -- it is genuinely new in round 3, concerns a file this PR already changed, and nobody has asked for it to be filed instead of fixed:

> **Major** -- `parse_response()` in `client.py:203` doesn't handle a 204 No Content response and raises a JSON-decode error instead of returning an empty result.

Triage this finding. Write your full reasoning (including which, if any, of the three named exceptions applies) and your fix/file/decline decision, to `outputs/triage.md`.
evals.expected_output: Explicitly states that none of the three named exceptions apply (not a direct instruction, not out-of-scope -- the PR already touches this file, not too large for a session), and the round budget (`max_rounds: 3`) is not yet exhausted at round 3. Routes the finding to the Fix path -- this is the core behavior change this redesign introduced: a round-3 finding is fixed by default, not automatically escalated to an issue just for arriving in round 3. Does not file this finding just because it's round 3.

evals.name: Reviewer-trigger ask after round 1, once for all remaining rounds
evals.prompt:
This is a simulated exercise: there is no real GitHub PR to fetch, and you must NOT attempt any `gh`/API calls, and you must NOT actually call AskUserQuestion -- instead, describe exactly what you would ask and why.

PR #170. Round 1 (triggered automatically by CI when the PR went ready-for-review) has just been fully triaged: one finding, fixed/verified/replied/resolved. `review_findings_min_rounds` is `1` (already satisfied) and `review_findings_max_rounds` is `3`. `review_findings_reviewers` has all three seed reviewers enabled with their default tracked trigger strings (Codex, CodeRabbit, Devin). This is the first time in this conversation that a next-round decision is being made.

Describe exactly what you would ask the user next, what options would be shown (including the exact literal text each option would post), and what you would do after the user answers. Write this to `outputs/decision.md`.
evals.expected_output: Since min_rounds is already satisfied but max_rounds is not, describes a single AskUserQuestion call carrying two questions rather than skipping straight to posting or asking a single combined question. Question 1: multi-select, one option per enabled reviewer (Codex, CodeRabbit, Devin) plus an explicit "No further round for now" option, never exceeding AskUserQuestion's real 4-option-per-question cap. Question 2: single-select, exactly 2 options ("Default review"/"Full review"), applied uniformly to whichever reviewer(s) Question 1 selects -- explicitly does NOT offer a separate default-vs-full pair of options per reviewer in Question 1, since 3 reviewers x 2 modes would exceed the 4-option cap. Correctly describes this as the first trigger-ask in the conversation, so it must actually ask rather than reuse a prior answer. States that if "No further round for now" is selected in Question 1, Question 2's answer is ignored and nothing is posted. States that after the user answers both questions, each selected reviewer's resolved trigger string gets validated (tracked-ness gate, then regex, then handle-token match) before anything is posted, and that this same decision will be reused for round 3 without asking again.

evals.name: Reviewer choice reused across rounds within the same conversation
evals.prompt:
This is a simulated exercise: there is no real GitHub PR to fetch, and you must NOT attempt any `gh`/API calls, and you must NOT actually call AskUserQuestion.

PR #170 (continuing from the same conversation as before). Earlier this conversation, after round 1, the user was asked and chose "Codex, full review" for all remaining rounds. Round 2 was triggered with `@codex full review`, Codex's round-2 findings are now fully triaged, and the round budget (`max_rounds: 3`) still allows round 3.

Descide what happens next regarding triggering round 3. Write your reasoning to `outputs/decision.md`.
evals.expected_output: States plainly that since the reviewer/mode choice was already made once this conversation (Codex, full review), it is NOT asked again before triggering round 3 -- the earlier answer is reused. States that the already-validated trigger string is reused as-is, without re-running the tracked-ness/regex/handle-token checks from scratch, since it was already validated earlier this conversation and no new, not-yet-validated reviewer/mode is being introduced here. Does not fabricate a new AskUserQuestion call for this round.

evals.name: Budget exhaustion with generate_issues:false -- fixed anyway
evals.prompt:
This is a simulated exercise: there is no real GitHub PR to fetch, and you must NOT attempt any `gh`/API calls. Given the review state described below, decide what to do and write your outputs to files instead of executing anything.

PR #180. `review_findings_max_rounds` is `3` and this skill has already triggered and triaged all 3 rounds it's allowed to trigger -- the round budget is exhausted. `review_findings_generate_issues` is `false` (the default). A human teammate leaves a new review comment against the current head:

> **Minor** -- a log message in `worker.py:44` still says "proccessing" (typo).

Triage this finding. Write your reasoning and decision to `outputs/triage.md`.
evals.expected_output: Recognizes the round budget is exhausted but, because `review_findings_generate_issues` is `false` (the default), fixes the finding anyway rather than filing it -- explicitly states the "fix everything" default holds even past the nominal round budget, since `max_rounds` only stops this skill from proactively triggering more rounds, it doesn't give a real finding a free pass. Does not treat budget exhaustion alone as equivalent to one of the three named exceptions.

evals.name: Reviewer trigger string fails handle-token validation -- excluded, falls back to tracked default
evals.prompt:
This is a simulated exercise: there is no real GitHub PR to fetch, and you must NOT attempt any `gh`/API calls, and you must NOT actually call AskUserQuestion -- instead, describe exactly what you would ask and why.

PR #190. Round 1 was just fully triaged and the round budget allows another round. `.claude/git-kit.local.json` is untracked (passes the tracked-ness gate) and overrides the `codex` entry in `review_findings_reviewers` to `default_review_trigger: "@codex-evil review"` -- everything else (coderabbit, devin) is unchanged from the tracked `git-kit.settings.json` defaults.

Describe what you would do when preparing the reviewer-trigger `AskUserQuestion`, specifically regarding the codex entry. Write this to `outputs/decision.md`.
evals.expected_output: Correctly identifies that `@codex-evil review` fails the handle-token check even though it contains "codex" as a substring -- the handle token right after `@` is `codex-evil`, which does not equal `codex` and does not match `^codex[a-z0-9]*$` (the hyphen breaks the match). States that this fails content validation (step 2 of the three-step check), so the skill falls back to the git-tracked `git-kit.settings.json` value for codex (`@codex review`) instead of using the untracked local override or silently accepting the lookalike. Does not offer `@codex-evil review` as an option, and does not exclude codex entirely from the ask, since a valid tracked fallback exists.

evals.name: codex-review-recovery's retry comment is excluded from the triggered-cycle count
evals.prompt:
This is a simulated exercise: there is no real GitHub PR to fetch, and you must NOT attempt any `gh`/API calls. Given the review state described below, decide what to do and write your outputs to files instead of executing anything.

PR #200. Round 1 was triggered automatically by CI and has already been fully triaged. `handling-review-findings` has not yet posted any trigger comment of its own on this PR. Separately, at some point after round 1, `codex-review-recovery` posted a plain top-level comment on this same PR reading exactly `@codex review` (with no trailing marker of any kind) -- this was a stuck-check recovery action (Codex's review had finished on its own dashboard but never posted back to GitHub), not a proactive round trigger from `handling-review-findings`. `review_findings_min_rounds` is `1`, `review_findings_max_rounds` is `3`.

Compute the current triggered-cycle count that Workflow step 8 would compare against `min_rounds`/`max_rounds`, and explain your reasoning in full. Write your answer to `outputs/count.md`.
evals.expected_output: States the triggered-cycle count is 1 (only round 1's automatic CI trigger), not 2. Explicitly states that the codex-review-recovery comment is excluded from the count because it carries no `<!-- handling-review-findings-trigger:<batch-id> -->` marker, even though its body text (`@codex review`) is byte-identical to what this skill's own Codex trigger would post. Does not conflate "matches a configured trigger string" with "this skill's own trigger" -- explicitly names the marker as the actual ownership signal, not the trigger-string text.

evals.name: A multi-reviewer selection counts as one triggered cycle, not one per reviewer
evals.prompt:
This is a simulated exercise: there is no real GitHub PR to fetch, and you must NOT attempt any `gh`/API calls, and you must NOT actually call AskUserQuestion.

PR #200. Round 1 (CI-triggered) has been fully triaged. The user was already asked (via the two-question trigger-ask) which reviewer(s)/mode to trigger for round 2, and selected both Codex and Devin (Question 1) with the Default review profile (Question 2). `review_findings_max_rounds` is `3`.

Describe exactly what gets posted for this decision (how many separate `gh pr comment` calls, and what each comment's body contains), and then describe how this decision affects the triggered-cycle count when a round-3 decision is later being made. Write your answer to `outputs/batch.md`.
evals.expected_output: Describes exactly 2 separate `gh pr comment` calls for this decision -- one for Codex (body: `@codex review` followed by a blank line and the marker), one for Devin (body: `/devin review` followed by a blank line and the marker) -- and explicitly states both comments carry the *same* `<batch-id>` value, generated once for this decision and reused verbatim across both posts, never a fresh id per reviewer. States plainly that when the triggered-cycle count is next computed, these two comments count as exactly ONE additional cycle (not two), because they share one batch-id -- so the count after this decision is 2 (1 for round 1, 1 for this two-reviewer round-2 batch), not 3. Does not describe counting per-comment.

evals.name: Below min_rounds, Question 1 omits the "No further round for now" option
evals.prompt:
This is a simulated exercise: there is no real GitHub PR to fetch, and you must NOT attempt any `gh`/API calls, and you must NOT actually call AskUserQuestion -- instead, describe exactly what you would ask and why.

PR #210. `review_findings_min_rounds` is `2` and `review_findings_max_rounds` is `3`. Round 1 (CI's automatic trigger) has just been fully triaged -- this is the only triggered cycle so far, so the current triggered-cycle count is `1`, which is below `min_rounds` (`2`). All three seed reviewers (Codex, CodeRabbit, Devin) are enabled with valid tracked trigger strings.

Describe exactly what Question 1 of the trigger-ask would offer as options in this situation, and explain why. Write your answer to `outputs/options.md`.
evals.expected_output: States that the current triggered-cycle count (1) is below `min_rounds` (2), so another cycle is mandatory -- proceeding without asking "whether," only "which." Describes Question 1 as offering *only* the three validated reviewer options (Codex, CodeRabbit, Devin), with **no** "No further round for now" option at all in this case -- explicitly states this option is omitted specifically because the floor hasn't been met yet, not merely because there happen to be exactly 3 reviewers. Contrasts this with the between-`min_rounds`-and-`max_rounds` case, where that stop option would normally appear as a 4th option. Does not offer a way to select "no round" while below the floor.

evals.name: gh api -f vs -F: does not use -f body=@<path>
evals.prompt: You need to reply to an inline PR review comment using `gh api repos/{owner}/{repo}/pulls/{pull_number}/comments/{comment_id}/replies`, per `references/github-api-mechanics.md`'s 'Replying to an inline PR review comment' section. The reply body is long (multi-paragraph, contains backticks and quotes) and has already been written to a scratchpad file at `/tmp/scratch/reply.txt`. Write the exact `gh api` command you would run to post this reply, and explain why you chose that exact form for passing the body. Save your answer to `outputs/command.md`.
evals.expected_output: Uses either `-f body="$(cat "/tmp/scratch/reply.txt")"` or `-F body=@/tmp/scratch/reply.txt` -- never `-f body=@/tmp/scratch/reply.txt`, which silently posts the literal string `@/tmp/scratch/reply.txt` as the comment body instead of the file's content. Explains that `-f`/`--raw-field` never interprets a leading `@` as a file reference -- only `-F`/`--field` does.

evals.name: Step 8 extraction: next-round-trigger.md read and followed, triggered-cycle count computed correctly
evals.prompt:
This is a simulated exercise: there is no real GitHub PR to fetch, and you must NOT attempt any `gh`/API calls. Given the review state described below, decide what to do and write your outputs to files instead of executing anything.

PR #220. Round 1 (CI-triggered) was fully triaged. Since then, you (this skill) posted exactly one round-2 trigger decision selecting Codex, whose comment carried marker `<!-- handling-review-findings-trigger:20260825T100000Z -->` authored by the account actually running this skill. A different GitHub user, unrelated to this skill's own trigger, separately posted a comment reading `@codex review` with no marker at all, on the same PR, at some other time. `review_findings_min_rounds` is `1`, `review_findings_max_rounds` is `3`.

Per your own Workflow step 8 (see `references/next-round-trigger.md` for the full procedure), compute the current triggered-cycle count and explain your reasoning. Write your answer to `outputs/count.md`.
evals.expected_output: States the triggered-cycle count is 2 (1 for round 1's automatic CI trigger, plus 1 for the single distinct batch-id marker from this skill's own round-2 trigger). Explicitly excludes the other user's markerless `@codex review` comment from the count, since it carries no `<!-- handling-review-findings-trigger:<batch-id> -->` marker authored by the account running this skill. Demonstrates the answer was derived by actually following references/next-round-trigger.md's 8a procedure (cites the marker-authorship check), not just guessing from the condensed SKILL.md pointer.

uncovered: A Critical finding first appears in round 3 and matches one of the three named exceptions (as opposed to arriving via budget exhaustion) -- filed, with the Hard Cap AskUserQuestion firing. Only the budget-exhaustion variant of this scenario is covered (eval 3); no eval exercises a Critical finding routed to the Issue path via exception 1/2/3 specifically in round 3.
A reviewer has enabled: false in review_findings_reviewers -- it never appears as an option in the trigger-ask. No eval constructs a disabled-reviewer scenario.

A fresh session (no memory of an earlier trigger-ask answer) triages what turns out to be round 3 and asks the reviewer/mode question again. Eval 15 only exercises the same-conversation reuse case, never the fresh-session contrast.

review_findings_max_rounds is reached and the skill's report states plainly that no further round will be triggered, with Workflow step 8 skipped entirely, as its own directly-asserted claim. Eval 16's own assertions cover the fix-vs-file routing at budget exhaustion, not this reporting/skip claim specifically -- it appears only incidentally in that eval's with_skill output, not as something any eval's metadata actually requires.

A reviewer entry's name field is malformed (uppercase, a regex metacharacter, or a path separator) and gets excluded from the trigger-ask before its trigger string is ever checked. No eval constructs a malformed-name scenario.

A review cycle comes back clean or produces only declined/filed findings (no fix-driven push), and the triggered-cycle count is still derived correctly from batch-marker history rather than the fix-driven-push round definition. No eval exercises a no-fix cycle against the budget check.

The user selects "No further round for now" in Question 1 together with a reviewer option, and Question 2's answer is correctly ignored. No eval exercises this combined-selection case specifically (eval 14 only exercises describing the options, not a combined selection being made).

The trigger-ask's two questions are answered but the commit(s) meant to be reviewed are still local-only (HEAD doesn't match the PR's headRefOid) -- no trigger comment gets posted. No eval exercises this precondition.
The trigger-ask's two questions are answered and the local commit is pushed, but the PR is a draft (or closed) -- no trigger comment gets posted. No eval exercises this precondition.

A tracked .claude/git-kit.local.json sets a reviewer's enabled: false -- 8c resolves the tracked-ness gate before touching enabled, so the tracked git-kit.settings.json default wins and the reviewer is still offered. No eval exercises this trust-boundary interaction for enabled specifically.

The max_rounds-th triggered batch's own review comes back with findings -- those findings are fixed normally even though 8a's count already reads max_rounds by classification time; they are not treated as post-budget. No eval exercises this final-cycle-vs-post-budget distinction.

A finding arrives from a human comment in a round after the round the max_rounds-th batch opened -- genuinely post-budget, routed per generate_issues. No eval exercises this specific later-round timing (distinct from eval 3/16's budget-exhaustion-by-count scenarios).

8c leaves exactly one reviewer surviving validation and the triggered-cycle count is below min_rounds -- Question 1 offers that reviewer plus the stop option (2 options, satisfying the AskUserQuestion minimum), but selecting stop reports the unmet floor rather than silently ending the run. No eval exercises this near-zero-reviewer edge case.
8c leaves zero reviewers surviving validation -- 8b's AskUserQuestion is skipped entirely and the run reports the configuration gap. No eval exercises this case.

A tracked .claude/git-kit.local.json sets severity_gate/generate_issues/max_rounds-lower-than-default -- each falls back to the tracked default too, same as enabled, with the run reporting which field(s) were discarded. No eval exercises this.

A tracked .claude/git-kit.local.json deletes a reviewer entry or sets review_findings_reviewers: [] -- the whole-array resolution means the tracked default's full roster is used regardless, never a per-entry join that lets a tracked file narrow the roster by omission. No eval exercises this.

The trust-boundary check is run from a subdirectory of the repo -- the root-anchored :/ pathspec still correctly reports a tracked file as tracked, unlike a bare relative pathspec which would wrongly report untracked and fail the boundary open. No eval exercises this (not a triage-decision behavior an eval can test without shell execution).

A human reviewer leaves an ordinary comment with no severity label or badge at all -- severity is classified from the described defect's actual content (round-and-dedup-rules.md's Hard Cap section), defaulting to Major (never Minor) when that content-based judgment is itself uncertain. No eval exercises this scenario, added 2026-08-29 (issue #95).
testing_validation_coverage.note: 28 named edge-case scenarios in references/testing-scenarios.md (post-redesign) -- up from 25 after a round-2 GitHub review on PR #101 (2026-08-22) found the triggered-cycle count couldn't distinguish this skill's own trigger comments from codex-review-recovery's identical-looking retry comment, and miscounted a multi-reviewer selection as one cycle per reviewer instead of one cycle total; fixed via a per-decision batch-id marker appended to every trigger comment, adding 3 new scenarios (recovery-comment exclusion, multi-reviewer batch-counts-once, below-min_rounds omits the stop option), none of which have eval coverage yet (added to uncovered below). The prior 25-scenario baseline (itself up from 20 after this session's round-1-review-response work: malformed reviewer name, the triggered-cycle-count/no-fix-cycle fix, the two-question redesign's combined-selection case, and the push/draft posting precondition x2; and before that, corrected from an earlier miscount of 15 by this skill's own reviewing-evals self-audit) is otherwise unchanged. Evals 14/15/17 cover reviewer-trigger/ask-once/validation scenarios not separately numbered in that file's prose list but described in its own text. A third round of live GitHub review on PR #101 (2026-08-22, reviewing commit 0e7a079) found the enabled:false filter ran before the tracked-ness trust-boundary check (a real regression from the same commit's own consistency-reviewer:C1 fix), no way to distinguish a final-allowed-cycle's own findings from genuinely post-budget ones, and no handling for fewer than 2 validated reviewers surviving 8c -- fixed by resolving the tracked-ness gate once and applying it to enabled and trigger text alike, redefining 'budget exhausted' as round-after-the-final-batch rather than count-at-ceiling, and adding an explicit fewer-than-2-reviewers path to 8b; adding 5 new scenarios, none of which have eval coverage yet (added to uncovered below). A same-day self-dispatched security-reviewer pass (required by .claude/rules/require-security-review-before-new-gate.md before shipping the enabled-vs-trust-boundary fix above) found the fix was too narrow: only 2 of 5 documented trust-boundary-protected fields ever had a real gate, the reviewer array's enabled protection was defeatable by deleting/replacing the whole array rather than flipping the flag, no disclosure was made when an override was discarded, and the git ls-files check itself failed open when run from a non-root working directory (live-verified). Fixed by hoisting the trust-boundary resolution to Settings-read time, protecting all four field-groups (severity_gate, generate_issues, max_rounds-lower, and the entire reviewers array as one unit -- never a per-field join), adding an explicit discard-disclosure requirement, and root-anchoring the git ls-files pathspec (:/ prefix) -- adding 3 more new scenarios, none of which have eval coverage yet. A 37th scenario was added 2026-08-29 (issue #95): the Hard Cap Exception severity fallback for a finding with no reviewer-stated severity label at all, defaulting to Major when the content-based judgment is itself uncertain -- no eval coverage yet, added to uncovered above.
